methodological_questions: Can role portability be compared between two role-defined subgroups with n=24 units?
Is the cut-heavy vs drive-heavy label reliable and independent of the portability outcome?
Does any difference in portability survive controls for destination context (landing-spot quality, coverage, teammates)?
Is the observed difference larger than profile-matched decoy or placebo benchmarks?

historical_evidence.finding: Portability confirmatory T1: a mover's displacement signature was more similar across franchises than profile-matched destination decoys' signatures. Median self_sim +0.129 vs decoy_sim +0.049, median Delta +0.0557, perm p=0.0050, 173/294 (58.8%) positive, sign p=2.87e-3, destination-franchise CI [+0.0192,+0.0859]. The record lists a PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE risk.

Destination net-rating checks for movers were recorded as 'underpowered and null once corrected for landing-spot quality'. Failure type A_unanswerable; limited by small sample and low power with a large MDE; dropped from Paper 1.

The A1 adaptation falsification tests found that an apparent adapter PPP lift was produced by a construction, selection or labelling flaw (C_artifact). The record cites label/classification error, selection or regression to the mean, LABEL_ERROR and MECHANICAL_FLOOR.
Coverage feasibility gate passed on 90 team-seasons (420,993 possessions). Coverage was separable from talent (|rho|=0.042). This concerns lineup coverage, not mover portability.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Mover-based test linking portability to destination outcome (net rating change).
failed_approaches.why: Underpowered (small sample, large MDE) and null once corrected for landing-spot quality; recorded as A_unanswerable.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Interpreting a group-level lift as a real effect when group labels were constructed from the outcome or by selection.
failed_approaches.why: Recorded as an artifact of construction, selection or labelling, with regression-to-the-mean and label-error limitations.

evidence_establishes: Per FAM:SF19 (supported), a portability measure (cross-franchise displacement-signature similarity versus profile-matched decoys) exists and showed a modest average positive effect among about 294-296 movers.
Per FAM:SF-PAP-029 (untestable), mover-based comparisons with small samples have previously been underpowered and confounded by landing-spot quality.
Per FAM:SF-APPA-001 (artifact), group contrasts built on labels derived from outcomes or selection have previously produced artifacts.
evidence_does_not_establish: Nothing retrieved compares cut-heavy with drive-heavy shapers, so the question as posed is not already answered.
The retrieved records do not show that the portability measure differs by role subtype or has adequate per-player reliability.
The records do not show how the n=24 units were defined or how many fall in each subgroup.
The records do not show whether a cut-heavy/drive-heavy label can be defined without using the outcome.
own_inferences: With n=24 split into about 12 per group, a two-group contrast can only detect very large effects (roughly d >= 1.2 at 80% power). The average portability effect in FAM:SF19 is small relative to its spread, so a subgroup difference is likely much smaller and undetectable.

Cut-heavy and drive-heavy shapers likely differ in position, usage and the teammates that make cutting or driving possible. Any difference in portability is therefore confounded with archetype and destination context.
Cut-heavy roles may look portable partly because cutting depends on teammates' passing, so context dependence could cut either way. The directional hypothesis has no strong prior.

If the portability measure is signature similarity, a role defined by the same displacement features could make 'cut-heavy' mechanically more or less self-similar. That would be an outcome-derived label and mechanical-floor artifact.
Role labels estimated from one team's season-sample are noisy. Extreme classifications regress toward the middle, and that can masquerade as poor portability.
uncertainties: How the 24 units are defined (movers, shapers, player-seasons) and how many are cut-heavy versus drive-heavy.
How 'travel' is operationalised, and whether a validated per-player portability measure exists beyond the FAM:SF19 aggregate.
Whether the threshold for 'heavy' is fixed in advance or data-driven.
I did not read the full family records, so details of FAM:SF19's decoy construction and clustering are limited to the retrieval summary.

historical_effect.explanation: Without history I might have proposed a direct two-group comparison. The untestable record on small mover samples (FAM:SF-PAP-029) and the artifact record on constructed labels (FAM:SF-APPA-001) push toward do_not_proceed as posed. FAM:SF19 supplies a usable portability measure and decoy benchmark, which is why a minimum viable alternative is specified.

blocking_constraints.text: n=24 split across two role groups gives an MDE of about 1.2 SD or more, far larger than the plausible subtype difference.
Per-player portability and role-share measures are noisy with few possessions per player-team stint.
Archetype is confounded with destination context, teammates and usage; the prior mover outcome test was null after landing-spot correction.

prior_work.summary: Aggregate mover portability was supported (FAM:SF19), but no retrieved record compares cut-heavy with drive-heavy shapers. Related small-sample mover work was untestable (FAM:SF-PAP-029), and a label-construction artifact was recorded (FAM:SF-APPA-001).

risks.text: n=24 with two subgroups; only very large differences are detectable, and a null would be uninformative.
Per-player role shares and portability scores rest on limited possessions on each side of the move.
Players classified as extreme cut-heavy or drive-heavy at origin regress toward the middle at destination. Selection into being a shaper and into moving adds further bias.
If role labels or the portability score share the same displacement or play-type features, subtype differences are partly mechanical.
Destination team scheme, teammates, minutes, position and age differ across the groups.
Derived play-type possession records from play-by-play may misclassify cuts and drives.
Portability is only meaningful relative to profile-matched decoys; the result depends on how the decoys are built.
Several cut/drive thresholds, seasons and portability metrics invite forking paths.
Role usage and league scheme change across 2022-23 to 2025-26, and the latest seasons are partly incomplete.

design.estimand: Difference in decoy-adjusted portability (self-similarity of the role signature across franchises minus matched-decoy similarity, as in FAM:SF19) per unit increase in origin cut share minus drive share, among shapers who change teams.
design.unit: Mover (shaper) with a pre-move and a post-move franchise stint, clustered by destination franchise.
design.sample: Minimum viable test: all shaper movers across 2022-23 to 2025-26 (complete seasons only for confirmatory use). Fix a minimum possession threshold per stint before looking at outcomes. Do not run the test unless at least about 80 qualifying movers exist. The current n=24 supports only descriptive reporting.
design.power: With n=24 in two groups (about 12 each), 80% power needs d >= about 1.2. A continuous moderator design needs roughly 80 or more movers to detect a correlation of about 0.3. Report the MDE before analysis; if n is below the threshold, label the result exploratory.
design.controls: Continuous cut-minus-drive share measured from origin-stint data, using a split-half or split-season reliability check and shrinkage to limit regression to the mean. Control for position, usage, minutes, age and destination team quality and scheme. Define role labels from features distinct from the portability signature, or recompute the signature excluding the cut and drive components.
design.falsification: Placebo moderator: shuffle role labels among movers within position; use profile-matched decoy destinations as in FAM:SF19; test non-movers' year-to-year role persistence as a check on mechanical effects; run an origin-only split-half test for label reliability.
design.multiplicity: One primary contrast (continuous cut-minus-drive moderator on decoy-adjusted portability). Thresholds and seasons are fixed in advance; secondary analyses are labelled exploratory and Holm-corrected.
design.decision_rule: Supported only if the moderator coefficient is positive with a destination-franchise-clustered 95% CI excluding 0, the permutation p is below 0.01 against shuffled labels, and the sign survives the context controls and the role-label reliability check. A CI containing 0 with an MDE above the plausible effect is reported as inconclusive, not rejected. A negative sign with the CI excluding 0 is reported as the reverse.
design.data_version: Per-game NBA stats API files, 2022-23 through 2025-26 regular seasons and playoffs, with the derived play-type possession graph. Freeze the data as of 2026-06-21 (playoff completion) and record the extraction date and graph build version before analysis.

methodological_questions: Do shaper roles persist when players change teams?
Is cut-heavy versus drive-heavy role classification reliable with small n?
How should role travel/portability be measured and compared between groups?
Is n=24 sufficient power for comparing two role groups?
Regression to the mean and selection in role classification

system_prompt:
You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Returns the most relevant consolidated study-family records of earlier research by this project that are available in this setting, with their identifiers; returns an empty list when none are available.
- glossary(): definitions of basketball and project terms used in task statements.
- data_catalog(): the fields available in each per-game data file.
- explore_graph(node_id): the relationships of one graph node (a family or a question, method, dataset, measure, limitation or risk node), with neighbour labels.
- read_family(id): the complete record of one study family (for example 'FAM:SF-APPA-001').

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace.

Risk codes (use only these): SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, RTM_SELECTION, OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, BASE_RATE, CONFOUNDING, LABEL_ERROR, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE, MULTIPLE_TESTING, IMPLEMENTATION_BUG, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY

- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): n=24

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

reasoning_details.text:
I'm weighing whether follow-up tool calls are worth it, since the budget allows, though I could also wrap up now. The question is whether cut-heavy shapers' roles travel better than drive-heavy ones, with only about 24 units, likely split into two groups of roughly 12, so the design looks underpowered. I'm also recalling the earlier SF19 portability confirmatory result with 296 movers, which used signature similarity.

I'm leaning toward not proceeding as the design is posed, since with only 24 units split into two groups the minimum detectable effect is large. The minimum viable version would be a continuous moderator across all shaper movers, and I'd keep my probabilities weighted toward untestable and uncertain.

I'm weighing whether follow-up tool calls are worth it, since the budget allows, though I could also wrap up now. The question is whether cut-heavy shapers' roles travel better than drive-heavy ones, with only about 24 units, likely split into two groups of roughly 12, so the design looks underpowered. I'm also recalling the earlier SF19 portability confirmatory result with 296 movers, which used signature similarity.

I'm leaning toward not proceeding as the design is posed, since with only 24 units split into two groups the minimum detectable effect is large. The minimum viable version would be a continuous moderator across all shaper movers, and I'd keep my probabilities weighted toward untestable and uncertain.
